examples.question_text: For a normally distributed dataset, use the empirical rule to estimate the probability that a randomly chosen score lies within $3$ standard deviations of the mean.
For a normally distributed dataset, use the empirical rule to estimate the probability that a randomly chosen score lies between the mean and $2$ standard deviations above the mean.
For a normally distributed dataset, use the empirical rule to estimate the probability that a randomly chosen score lies more than $3$ standard deviations below the mean.
For a normally distributed dataset, use the empirical rule to estimate the percentage of scores between $2$ and $3$ standard deviations above the mean.
For a normally distributed dataset, use the empirical rule to estimate the percentage of scores greater than $1$ standard deviation below the mean.

For a normally distributed dataset, use the empirical rule to estimate the probability that a randomly chosen score lies between $1$ standard deviation below the mean and $3$ standard deviations above the mean.

Test scores are normally distributed with a mean of $64$ and a standard deviation of $4$. Use the empirical rule to estimate the percentage of scores:
(a) between $56$ and $72$
(b) between $52$ and $68$
(c) below $56$.

The times taken by a machine to complete a cycle are normally distributed with a mean of $42$ seconds and a standard deviation of $4$ seconds. One cycle takes $54$ seconds. Use the empirical rule to decide whether this is unusually long.

methods.description: Read the approximate 68%, 95% or 99.7% central percentage for an interval within one, two or three standard deviations.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 6 Standard/The Normal Distribution 3_Probability using z-scores.md lines 59–67; Foundation Q1(a), lines 117–122

methods.description: Use symmetry to halve a central percentage for an interval from the mean to a whole-number standard-deviation boundary.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 6 Standard/The Normal Distribution 3_Probability using z-scores.md lines 59–71; Example, lines 83–92; Foundation Q1(b), lines 117–122

methods.description: Subtract a central percentage from 100% and halve the remainder to obtain one tail.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 6 Standard/The Normal Distribution 3_Probability using z-scores.md lines 59–79; empirical-rule practice (b), lines 94–105; Foundation Q1(e,i), lines 123–132

methods.description: Subtract two half-band percentages to obtain an interval between standard-deviation boundaries on the same side of the mean.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 6 Standard/The Normal Distribution 3_Probability using z-scores.md lines 59–71; Foundation Q1(g,h), lines 128–132

methods.description: Add a half-band percentage to the 50% on the other side of the mean to obtain a one-sided cumulative percentage.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 6 Standard/The Normal Distribution 3_Probability using z-scores.md lines 59–79; empirical-rule practice (a), lines 94–105; Foundation Q1(c,f), lines 117–127

methods.description: Split an interval crossing the mean into two half-bands and add their percentages.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 6 Standard/The Normal Distribution 3_Probability using z-scores.md lines 59–71; empirical-rule practice (c), lines 94–105; Foundation Q1(d), lines 123–127

methods.description: Identify supplied numerical boundaries as whole numbers of standard deviations from the mean, then apply the relevant empirical-rule region method.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 6 Standard/The Normal Distribution 3_Probability using z-scores.md Foundation Q1(a–i), lines 109–132

methods.description: Use an outcome's distance from the mean and its small empirical-rule tail percentage to justify an unusual-outcome judgement.
